q: What is zero trust and how does it relate to what we do?
a: Zero trust: no implicit trust based on network location — every access is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted, with least privilege and continuous verification (NIST SP 800-207 is the reference architecture). It shows up here as identity-first design, micro-segmentation, and the IAM non-negotiables on Engineering — every reference architecture there assumes zero-trust rather than perimeter trust.

q: What is least privilege and why is it repeated in every design review?
a: Least privilege: every identity (human or service) gets the minimum access needed, for the minimum time needed. It is one of the non-negotiables on Engineering because it limits blast radius — when something is compromised, damage stops at what that identity could touch. It is also why the access workflow (Tools & Dashboards) requires named sponsorship and periodic recertification rather than permanent broad grants.

q: What is defense in depth (layers)?
a: Never rely on a single control: layers of independent defenses (network segmentation, host hardening, identity controls, monitoring, physical security) so the failure of one layer does not become the failure of the mission. The reference architectures on Engineering implement it visibly — enclave edge, host STIGs, identity gates, and monitoring each assume another layer could fail.

q: What does MFA actually protect against (and what does it not)?
a: MFA stops the most common attack path — a stolen password alone is not enough — which is why it is a baseline requirement across our reference architectures. It does not stop everything: MFA-fatigue prompt bombs, SIM swaps on SMS-based second factors, and session-token theft all bypass specific implementations. Strong pairing (FIDO2/smartcard over SMS) matters; the phishing case that still succeeds is where watch-desk speed kicks in.

q: What is phishing and how do I spot it?
a: Fraudulent messages engineered to harvest credentials or deliver malware — the top intrusion vector. Spot it by: urgency and secrecy, mismatched sender domains, unexpected attachments, and links whose destinations do not match their text (hover before clicking). If you already clicked, entered credentials, or opened the attachment — that is the phishing exception: treat it as malware and call the watch desk immediately (Incident Response). No-click phishing reports: within 4 hours. The Phishing Analysis agent is in the Agent Catalog.

q: What is CVSS and does it decide severity?
a: CVSS scores technical severity of a vulnerability (0–10) from exploitability and impact metrics. It feeds prioritization but does not decide our response severity alone: the SLA clock keys off CAT/KEV status, and mission context (criticality, exposure, compensating posture) can move the operational verdict — that is the CVE-to-mission translation on Risk Management. A CVSS 9.8 on an air-gapped training simulator and a 5.0 on an internet-facing CUI system can invert in real priority.

q: What is the difference between vulnerability scanning and penetration testing?
a: Scanning (ACAS/Nessus) is broad, automated, and scheduled weekly — it enumerates known weaknesses. Penetration testing is scoped, manual, and adversarial — it explores paths a scanner cannot reason about. Both appear in our ecosystem: scans for steady-state cadence, pentest capability in the Tier II Intermediate Pentest course (Training Academy). Findings from either feed the same SLA/POA&M pipeline (Vulnerability & POA&M).
